title: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable stabilizer codes
formal: Do there exist constants \(r,\delta ,s>0\) and integers \(w,b\ge 1\), and stabilizer codes Q on unbounded numbers n of qubits, such that Q encodes at least rn logical qubits, has distance at least \(\delta n\), every listed check has weight at most w, every qubit occurs in at most b checks, and the normalized check Hamiltonian satisfies \(H\succeq (s/n)D_{Q}\)?
definitions: Use the Hilbert space \((\mathbb{C} ^{2})\otimes n\). On a computational basis bit, X flips the bit and Z multiplies |\(1\rangle\) by −1 while fixing |\(0\rangle ; Y\)=iXZ. A Pauli operator is a tensor product of I,X,Y,Z, up to phase, and its weight is the number of nonidentity tensor factors. A listed check \(S_{j}\) is a nonidentity Hermitian Pauli operator with eigenvalues ±1. The \(m\ge 1\) checks commute, and the group they generate must not contain −I. Their joint +1 eigenspace Q has dimension \(2^{k}\), where k is the number of encoded logical qubits. Code distance d is the minimum weight of a Pauli operator that preserves Q but whose restriction to Q is not a scalar multiple of the identity. Checks may be redundant; both the weight bound and the per-qubit incidence bound refer to the listed checks. Define \(H=(1/m)\sum_{j=1}^{m}(I- S_{j})/2\). For \(0\le t\le n\), let \(Q_{t}\) be the linear span of \(E|\psi \rangle\) over all |\(\psi \rangle \in Q\) and Pauli errors E of weight at most t, and let \(\Pi _{t}\) be the orthogonal projector onto \(Q_{t}\). Define \(D_{Q}=\sum_{t=0}^{n- 1}(I- \Pi _{t})\). The operator inequality \(H\succeq (s/n)D_{Q}\) means that its difference is positive semidefinite, or equivalently that the corresponding expectation inequality holds for every quantum state. All five constants are fixed independently of n, and \(k\ge rn\) and \(d\ge \delta n\) must hold throughout an infinite family with \(n\to \infty\). This card uses the bounded-degree stabilizer version of qLTC existence. Checks need not be geometrically local, and no efficient construction algorithm is required.
answer_criterion: Construct or prove existence of an infinite family satisfying all the stated conditions with fixed constants, or prove that every family of stabilizer presentations fails at least one of them. The target requires maximum check weight and qubit incidence to be bounded, not merely their averages. Inverse-polylogarithmic soundness or relative distance does not qualify. Verifying soundness only for some low-weight errors is insufficient: the operator inequality must hold on the entire Hilbert space.
why: A central missing object connecting quantum error correction to robust verification. It asks whether sparse quantum constraints can simultaneously protect a linear amount of information and detect global corruption with constant normalized soundness.

importance.reason: A defining construction problem beyond good quantum LDPC codes, with direct links to local testing, Hamiltonian complexity, fault tolerance and the quantum PCP program.

progress.text: Panteleev–Kalachev construct good quantum LDPC codes and, separately, good classical LTCs.
Anshu–Breuckmann–Nirkhe resolve NLTS using good quantum codes without constructing good constant-soundness qLTCs.
Cross and coauthors publish constant-soundness qLTCs with compromises in distance, rate or maximum locality.
Wills–Lin–Hsieh analyze soundness under general distance balancing.
The corrected Dinur–Lin–Vidick version achieves constant rate and locality with \(\log ^{3}n\) losses in relative distance and soundness.
Sun–Vidick apply qLTCs to quantum interactive oracle proofs with polylogarithmic query complexity.
Li–Li–Liu replace the invalid April argument and retain transversal-gate claims for almost-good codes.

status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No bounded-degree stabilizer family with constant rate, relative distance and normalized soundness was located. The corrected 2025 and July 2026 constructions retain inverse-polylogarithmic losses, while constant-soundness variants increase locality or sacrifice other parameters.

context_blocks.text: A quantum code is the common accepting space of many checks. Measuring a uniformly selected check rejects a state with probability equal to its expected normalized energy under H. Local testability asks for a robust version of exact membership: a state that requires many local changes to reach the code must violate a noticeable fraction of checks. Constant check weight then makes this a test involving only a constant number of qubits.

Distance from the code must account for quantum degeneracy. A large Pauli operator can be a stabilizer and leave every encoded state unchanged; another can implement a logical operation while still remaining inside the code space. Neither should be called far from the code merely because its written support is large. The spaces \(Q_{t}\) and the operator \(D_{Q}\) measure how many physical qubits are needed to leave the entire code space in each orthogonal error sector. The soundness condition also covers superpositions and mixed states.

A simple classical analogy illustrates the missing property. Consider a chain of equality checks requiring adjacent bits to agree. A string consisting of a long zero block followed by a long one block can be far from either valid repetition-code word while violating only one check. Local constraints and even a large code distance therefore do not by themselves imply robust local testing. The quantum target additionally requires storing a linear number of logical qubits.

Panteleev and Kalachev resolved the existence of asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes: constant check size can coexist with constant rate and linear distance. Their work also establishes good locally testable classical codes. These are two different conclusions. Quantum local testability with constant soundness does not follow by combining the words in the paper’s title; it is the extra property sought here.

Cross and coauthors obtain constant-soundness qLTC constructions with other parameter compromises. One approach has distance growing with check locality; another has constant average locality while some checks and qubit incidences grow. Wills, Lin and Hsieh analyze distance balancing with more general classical ingredients, quantifying the accompanying soundness loss. Such tradeoffs make it important to track the maximum locality, normalized soundness, rate and distance simultaneously.

Dinur, Lin and Vidick’s construction comes much closer: it has \(k=\Omega (n)\), distance \(\Omega (n/\log ^{3}n)\), soundness \(\Omega (1/\log ^{3}n)\), and constant check size. Its September 2025 revision corrects the rate analysis by shifting the chain complex. The paper also describes ways to obtain constant soundness, and then linear distance, at the cost of polylogarithmic check size. These variants do not provide all the constants required by this card at once.

The NLTS theorem is another nearby achievement with a distinct conclusion. Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe show that certain good quantum codes yield Hamiltonians whose low-energy states require nontrivial circuit depth to prepare. That theorem resolves a major quantum-complexity conjecture without establishing constant-soundness local testability. A qLTC would give a stronger relation between energy and distance from a code, and could support further work toward quantum PCP; it would not by itself prove the full quantum PCP conjecture.

Li, Li and Liu’s July 2026 revision adds transversal non-Clifford operations to almost-good constructions. For example, their three-qubit controlled-controlled-Z case retains logarithmic losses in distance and soundness. The revision replaces an invalid cap-product argument from April with a substantially different proof using product-expanding local codes. This adds computational functionality while leaving the constant-parameter qLTC question open.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 work uses qLTCs in interactive oracle proofs for QMA, with polynomial communication and polylogarithmically many queried qubits. It illustrates the value of the available approximate parameters. Interaction and a polylogarithmic query budget remain part of that result; it is not a constant-query static quantum PCP or a construction meeting the stronger code parameters here.

sentences: A locally testable quantum code should reveal a substantial error by checking only a few qubits.
The desired family must also encode a linear amount of quantum information and tolerate errors on a linear number of physical qubits.
Each check and each qubit's participation in checks must remain bounded as the code grows.
These requirements strengthen ordinary good quantum LDPC codes by demanding a quantitative relation between distance from the code space and rejection probability.
Such codes would connect robust quantum error detection with the complexity of low-energy states and the broader search for quantum PCP constructions.
